claim: Between 1980 and 2013, the number of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds increased by a factor of 9.3.
source: Between 1980 and 2013, the number of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds increased by a factor of 9.3, compared with a 2.6-fold increase in the number of PhD graduates from WR groups.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a direct finding from analysis of National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates data, as shown in Figure 1Ai-ii.

claim: Between 1980 and 2013, the number of PhD graduates from WR backgrounds increased by a factor of 2.6.
source: Between 1980 and 2013, the number of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds increased by a factor of 9.3, compared with a 2.6-fold increase in the number of PhD graduates from WR groups.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a direct finding from analysis of National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates data, as shown in Figure 1Bi-ii.

claim: The number of scientists from URM backgrounds hired as assistant professors in medical school basic science departments was not related to the number of potential candidates (R2=0.12, p>0.07).
source: However, the number of scientists from URM backgrounds hired as assistant professors in medical school basic science departments was not related to the number of potential candidates (R2=0.12, p>0.07), whereas there was a strong correlation between these two numbers for scientists from WR backgrounds (R2=0.48, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of hiring data from AAMC Faculty Roster and PhD graduate data from NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 2Aii.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the number of potential WR candidates and the number of WR scientists hired as assistant professors (R2=0.48, p<0.0001).
source: However, the number of scientists from URM backgrounds hired as assistant professors in medical school basic science departments was not related to the number of potential candidates (R2=0.12, p>0.07), whereas there was a strong correlation between these two numbers for scientists from WR backgrounds (R2=0.48, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of hiring data from AAMC Faculty Roster and PhD graduate data from NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: The system dynamics model explained 79% of the variance in the hiring of assistant professors.
source: We built and validated a conceptual system dynamics model based on these data that explained 79% of the variance in the hiring of assistant professors and posited no hiring discrimination.
evidence: Model validation results comparing model predictions to empirical data, as shown in Figure 4Aiii.

claim: The system dynamics model posited no hiring discrimination.
source: We built and validated a conceptual system dynamics model based on these data that explained 79% of the variance in the hiring of assistant professors and posited no hiring discrimination.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure described in the methods and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Given current transition rates of scientists from URM backgrounds to faculty positions, faculty diversity would not increase significantly through the year 2080 even in the context of exponential growth in the population of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds.
source: Simulations show that, given current transition rates of scientists from URM backgrounds to faculty positions, faculty diversity would not increase significantly through the year 2080 even in the context of an exponential growth in the population of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds, or significant increases in the number of faculty positions.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Bi and 5Bii.

claim: Faculty diversity would not increase significantly through 2080 even with significant increases in the number of faculty positions, given current transition rates.
source: Simulations show that, given current transition rates of scientists from URM backgrounds to faculty positions, faculty diversity would not increase significantly through the year 2080 even in the context of an exponential growth in the population of PhD graduates from URM backgrounds, or significant increases in the number of faculty positions.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Bi and 5Bii.

claim: Diversity increased as more postdoctoral candidates from URM backgrounds transitioned onto the market and were hired.
source: Instead, the simulations showed that diversity increased as more postdoctoral candidates from URM backgrounds transitioned onto the market and were hired.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Aiii, 5Aiv, 5Biii, and 5Biv.

claim: Scientists from URM backgrounds receive 6% of NIH research project grants.
source: Scientists from certain underrepresented minority (URM) racial/ethnic backgrounds—specifically, African American/Black, Hispanic/Latin@, American Indian, and Alaska Native—receive 6% of NIH research project grants (Ginther et al., 2016, 2011; National Institutes of Health, 2012b) despite having higher representation in the relevant labor market (Heggeness et al., 2016), and constituting 32% of the US population (National Institutes of Health, 2012b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ginther et al., 2016, 2011; National Institutes of Health, 2012b).

claim: Scientists from URM backgrounds have higher representation in the relevant labor market than their 6% share of NIH research project grants.
source: Scientists from certain underrepresented minority (URM) racial/ethnic backgrounds—specifically, African American/Black, Hispanic/Latin@, American Indian, and Alaska Native—receive 6% of NIH research project grants (Ginther et al., 2016, 2011; National Institutes of Health, 2012b) despite having higher representation in the relevant labor market (Heggeness et al., 2016), and constituting 32% of the US population (National Institutes of Health, 2012b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Heggeness et al., 2016).

claim: URM populations constitute 32% of the US population.
source: Scientists from certain underrepresented minority (URM) racial/ethnic backgrounds—specifically, African American/Black, Hispanic/Latin@, American Indian, and Alaska Native—receive 6% of NIH research project grants (Ginther et al., 2016, 2011; National Institutes of Health, 2012b) despite having higher representation in the relevant labor market (Heggeness et al., 2016), and constituting 32% of the US population (National Institutes of Health, 2012b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Institutes of Health, 2012b).

claim: Approximately 83% of NIH funding is awarded to investigators at extramural institutions.
source: The vast majority of NIH funding—approximately 83%—is awarded to investigators at extramural institutions, many of whom serve as faculty members at academic and research institutions (Johnson, 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Johnson, 2013).

claim: Medical schools that belong to the AAMC receive 67% of NIH extramural funding.
source: In particular, MD-granting medical schools and their affiliates (henceforth, medical schools) that belong to the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) receive 67% of NIH extramural funding, and comprised the entire top 20 of NIH-funded institutions in FY2015 (National Institutes of Health, 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Institutes of Health, 2016).

claim: Medical schools that belong to the AAMC comprised the entire top 20 of NIH-funded institutions in FY2015.
source: In particular, MD-granting medical schools and their affiliates (henceforth, medical schools) that belong to the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) receive 67% of NIH extramural funding, and comprised the entire top 20 of NIH-funded institutions in FY2015 (National Institutes of Health, 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Institutes of Health, 2016).

claim: Diversifying faculties is perhaps the least successful of the diversity initiatives.
source: However, a 2011 report from the National Academies of Sciences said "diversifying faculties is perhaps the least successful of the diversity initiatives" (National Academy of Sciences, 2011).
evidence: Direct quote from National Academy of Sciences report (National Academy of Sciences, 2011).

claim: Student protests on college campuses in the 2015 academic year often centered on the need for more faculty diversity.
source: Student protests on college campuses across the country in the 2015 academic year often centered on the need for more faculty diversity, and highlighted the lack thereof, especially in scientific disciplines (Griffin, 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Griffin, 2016).

claim: The annual number of URM PhD graduates grew from n=93 in 1980 to n=868 in 2013.
source: The annual number of URM PhD graduates grew more than nine-fold from 1980–2013 (from n=93 to n=868), whereas the population of URM assistant professors grew 2.6-fold (from n=132 in 1980 to n=341 in 2014; Figure 1Ai–ii).
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 1Ai.

claim: The population of URM assistant professors grew from n=132 in 1980 to n=341 in 2014.
source: The annual number of URM PhD graduates grew more than nine-fold from 1980–2013 (from n=93 to n=868), whereas the population of URM assistant professors grew 2.6-fold (from n=132 in 1980 to n=341 in 2014; Figure 1Ai–ii).
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster, as shown in Figure 1Ai.

claim: The annual number of WR PhD graduates grew from n=3989 in 1980 to n=8789 in 2013.
source: In comparison, for scientists from WR backgrounds growth in assistant professors was more closely aligned with growth in PhD graduates–there was a 2.2-fold increase in the annual number of PhD graduates (from n=3989 in 1980 to n=8789 in 2013; Figure 1Bi–ii), and a 1.7-fold increase for population of assistant professors (n=3246 in 1980 to n=5562 in 2014; Figure 1Bi–ii).
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 1Bi.

claim: The population of WR assistant professors grew from n=3246 in 1980 to n=5562 in 2014.
source: In comparison, for scientists from WR backgrounds growth in assistant professors was more closely aligned with growth in PhD graduates–there was a 2.2-fold increase in the annual number of PhD graduates (from n=3989 in 1980 to n=8789 in 2013; Figure 1Bi–ii), and a 1.7-fold increase for population of assistant professors (n=3246 in 1980 to n=5562 in 2014; Figure 1Bi–ii).
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster, as shown in Figure 1Bi.

claim: There was a statistically significant interaction between URM status and position (β=1.60; p=3.6*10−7; PhD graduates relative to assistant professors).
source: That is, there was a statistically significant interaction between URM status and position (β=1.60; p=3.6*10−7; PhD graduates relative to assistant professors), above the impacts URM status (β=0.0602, p=0.005), position alone (β = 0.229, p=0.28), or the increases that occurred as the system grew through time (β = 0.0895, p=2*10−16).
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear regression model on PhD graduate and assistant professor population data.

claim: Among U.S. citizens and permanent residents, the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.5% in 1980 to 13% in 2013.
source: Among the pool of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.5% in 1980 to 13% in 2013, whereas in the overall pool the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.3% in 1980 to 9% in 2013.
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 1Aiii.

claim: In the overall pool, the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.3% in 1980 to 9% in 2013.
source: Among the pool of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.5% in 1980 to 13% in 2013, whereas in the overall pool the proportion of URM PhD graduates grew from 2.3% in 1980 to 9% in 2013.
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates, as shown in Figure 1Aiii.

claim: The percentage of URM assistant professors grew from 3.9% in 1980 to 5.8% in 2014.
source: In contrast, the percentage of URM assistant professors grew from 3.9% in 1980 to 5.8% in 2014 (Figure 1Aiii).
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster, as shown in Figure 1Aiii.

claim: Between 2005-2013, a total of 5,842 biomedical PhDs were awarded to scientists from URM backgrounds.
source: Between 2005-2013, a total of 5,842 biomedical PhDs were awarded to scientists from URM backgrounds; however, there were six fewer URM assistant professors in basic science departments in 2014 than in 2005 (n=341 in 2014 versus 347 in 2005).
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates.

claim: There were six fewer URM assistant professors in basic science departments in 2014 than in 2005 (n=341 in 2014 versus 347 in 2005).
source: Between 2005-2013, a total of 5,842 biomedical PhDs were awarded to scientists from URM backgrounds; however, there were six fewer URM assistant professors in basic science departments in 2014 than in 2005 (n=341 in 2014 versus 347 in 2005).
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster.

claim: For scientists from WR backgrounds, there was 31% growth in the annual number of PhD graduates between 2005 and 2013 (n=8789 in 2013 compared to n=6703 in 2005).
source: For scientists from WR backgrounds, there was 31% growth in the annual number of PhD graduates (n=8789 in 2013 compared to n=6703 in 2005) and 8.6% growth in the population of assistant professors (n=5562 in 2014 compared to n=5122 in 2005).
evidence: Data from National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates.

claim: For scientists from WR backgrounds, there was 8.6% growth in the population of assistant professors between 2005 and 2014 (n=5562 in 2014 compared to n=5122 in 2005).
source: For scientists from WR backgrounds, there was 31% growth in the annual number of PhD graduates (n=8789 in 2013 compared to n=6703 in 2005) and 8.6% growth in the population of assistant professors (n=5562 in 2014 compared to n=5122 in 2005).
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster.

claim: For scientists from URM backgrounds, there was a 7.6-fold increase in the size of the potential candidate pool.
source: For scientists from URM backgrounds, there was a 7.6-fold increase in the size of the potential candidate pool (Figure 2Ai); however, the size of the potential URM candidate pool was not significantly correlated with the number of URM assistant professors hired each year (R2=0.12, p=0.07; Figure 2Aii).
evidence: Calculated from PhD graduate and hiring data, as shown in Figure 2Ai.

claim: For scientists from WR backgrounds, there was a 2.2-fold growth in the size of the candidate pool.
source: In contrast, for scientists from WR backgrounds there was a 2.2-fold growth in the size of the candidate pool (Figure 2Bi), and the size of the potential candidate pool was significantly correlated with the number of assistant professors hired (R2=0.48, p=2.54*10−5; Figure 2Bii).
evidence: Calculated from PhD graduate and hiring data, as shown in Figure 2Bi.

claim: For scientists from URM backgrounds, the proportion of the candidate pool hired into assistant professor positions decreased from year to year (β=-0.14, p=9.6*10−4).
source: For scientists from URM backgrounds, the proportion of the candidate pool hired into assistant professor positions decreased from year to year (β=-0.14, p=9.6*10−4), while for scientists from WR backgrounds the proportion of the potential candidate pool hired did not change significantly over time (β=0.004, p=0.77).
evidence: Statistical analysis of hiring data, as shown in Figure 2Aiii.

claim: For scientists from WR backgrounds, the proportion of the potential candidate pool hired did not change significantly over time (β=0.004, p=0.77).
source: For scientists from URM backgrounds, the proportion of the candidate pool hired into assistant professor positions decreased from year to year (β=-0.14, p=9.6*10−4), while for scientists from WR backgrounds the proportion of the potential candidate pool hired did not change significantly over time (β=0.004, p=0.77).
evidence: Statistical analysis of hiring data, as shown in Figure 2Biii.

claim: The model captured 51% of the variance in URM hiring (R2=0.51, p<0.0001).
source: When disaggregated by URM and WR status, the model captures 51% of the variance in URM hiring (Figure 4Biii; R2=0.51, p<0.0001), and 78% of the variance in WR assistant professor hiring (R2=0.78, p<0.0001; Figure 4Ciii).
evidence: Model validation results comparing model predictions to empirical data, as shown in Figure 4Biii.

claim: The model captured 78% of the variance in WR assistant professor hiring (R2=0.78, p<0.0001).
source: When disaggregated by URM and WR status, the model captures 51% of the variance in URM hiring (Figure 4Biii; R2=0.51, p<0.0001), and 78% of the variance in WR assistant professor hiring (R2=0.78, p<0.0001; Figure 4Ciii).
evidence: Model validation results comparing model predictions to empirical data, as shown in Figure 4Ciii.

claim: In 2014, 5.8% of assistant professors in basic science departments were from URM backgrounds.
source: In 2014, 5.8% of assistant professors in basic science departments were from URM backgrounds.
evidence: Data from AAMC Faculty Roster.

claim: The 5.8% representation of URM assistant professors in 2014 is consistent with a transition rate of 0.25% of 'other aspire' URM PhDs onto the market.
source: This level of representation is consistent with a transition rate of 0.25% of "other aspire" URM PhDs onto the market (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Model calibration result matching empirical data.

claim: By 2030, the model predicted that 13.8% of biomedical PhDs would be URMs.
source: Specifically, the model predicted that by 2030, 13.8% of biomedical PhDs would be URMs, but that only 5.9% of assistant professors would be URMs whether the number of assistant professor positions remained the same (Figure 5Ai) or grew by 100 positions annually beginning in 2015 (Figure 5Aii).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Ai and 5Aii.

claim: By 2030, the model predicted that only 5.9% of assistant professors would be URMs if the number of assistant professor positions remained the same and the transition rate stayed at 0.25%.
source: Specifically, the model predicted that by 2030, 13.8% of biomedical PhDs would be URMs, but that only 5.9% of assistant professors would be URMs whether the number of assistant professor positions remained the same (Figure 5Ai) or grew by 100 positions annually beginning in 2015 (Figure 5Aii).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Ai.

claim: By 2030, the model predicted that only 5.9% of assistant professors would be URMs even if the number of positions grew by 100 annually beginning in 2015, given a 0.25% transition rate.
source: Specifically, the model predicted that by 2030, 13.8% of biomedical PhDs would be URMs, but that only 5.9% of assistant professors would be URMs whether the number of assistant professor positions remained the same (Figure 5Ai) or grew by 100 positions annually beginning in 2015 (Figure 5Aii).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Aii.

claim: Increasing the transition rate to 10% increased URM representation in the assistant professor pool to between 12.4–12.5% in 2030.
source: Increasing the transition rate to 10% increased URM representation in the assistant professor pool to between 12.4–12.5% in 2030 given the same (Figure 5Aiii) or increased number of positions available (Figure 5Aiv).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Aiii and 5Aiv.

claim: If the URM PhD population continued to grow at an exponential rate through 2080, 73% of PhDs would be URMs.
source: The model predicted if the URM PhD population continued to grow at an exponential rate through 2080, 73% of PhDs would be URMs (at which point these populations would no longer be underrepresented).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Bi and 5Bii.

claim: In the presence of the 0.25% transition rate, the model predicted that in 2080 fewer than 10% of assistant professors would be URMs, no matter the number of positions available.
source: However, in the presence of the 0.25% transition rate, the model predicted that in 2080 fewer than 10% of assistant professors would be URMs, no matter the number of positions available (Figure 5Bi and Bii).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Bi and 5Bii.

claim: If the transition rate increased to 10%, URM assistant professor representation would be between 56.5-58.3% in 2080.
source: In contrast, the simulations predicted that if the transition rate increased to 10%, URM assistant professor representation would be between 56.5-58.3% given the same (Figure 5Biii) or increased number of positions available (Figure 5Biv).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5Biii and 5Biv.

claim: Following the doubling of the NIH budget between 1998 and 2003, there was a significant increase in the number of PhDs awarded, without commensurate increase in the number of faculty positions.
source: Following the doubling of the NIH budget between 1998 and 2003, there was a significant increase in the number of PhDs awarded, without commensurate increase in the number of faculty positions (Stephan, 2012; Alberts et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Stephan, 2012; Alberts et al., 2014).

claim: It is estimated that fewer than 11% of all life science PhDs enter faculty positions in any institution type.
source: Further, it is estimated that fewer than 11% of all life science PhDs enter faculty positions in any institution type (National Science Board, 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Science Board, 2014).

claim: Graduate students and postdocs from all backgrounds lose interest in faculty careers in research-intensive universities as their training progresses.
source: Beyond the number of faculty positions available, there is evidence that graduate students and postdocs from all backgrounds lose interest in faculty careers in research-intensive universities as their training progresses (Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2015; Sauermann and Roach, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2015; Sauermann and Roach, 2012).

claim: At PhD completion, URM men and women report lower levels of interest in faculty positions at research-intensive universities than their WR counterparts, even when controlling for career interests at PhD entry, scholarly productivity, mentorship or research self-efficacy.
source: Moreover, at PhD completion URM men and women report lower levels of interest in faculty positions at research-intensive universities than their WR counterparts, even when controlling for career interests at PhD entry, scholarly productivity, mentorship or research self-efficacy (Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gibbs et al., 2014).

claim: Increasing diversity in the applicant pool and equitable evaluation in the hiring process are strategies that promote faculty diversity.
source: Increasing diversity in the applicant pool and equitable evaluation in the hiring process are strategies that promote faculty diversity (Turner, 2002; Sheridan et al., 2010; Moody, 2004; Smith, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Turner, 2002; Sheridan et al., 2010; Moody, 2004; Smith, 2015).

claim: The chair of a recent faculty search in systems biology at Harvard university reported very low numbers of applications from women and scientists from URM backgrounds.
source: While systematic data are not available on the demographics of faculty applicants, the chair of a recent faculty search in systems biology at Harvard university reported very low numbers of applications from women and scientists from URM backgrounds (Eddy, 2015), lending credence to the notion that faculty applicant pools lack diversity.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Eddy, 2015).

claim: System Dynamics has been used to examine the macro-scale impacts of potential policy interventions on the biomedical postdoctoral workforce.
source: In particular, computational modeling approaches such as System Dynamics (SD) have been used to examine the macro-scale impacts of potential policy interventions on the biomedical postdoctoral workforce (Ghaffarzadegan et al., 2014), and new faculty hiring (Larson and Diaz, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ghaffarzadegan et al., 2014).

claim: System Dynamics has been used to examine new faculty hiring.
source: In particular, computational modeling approaches such as System Dynamics (SD) have been used to examine the macro-scale impacts of potential policy interventions on the biomedical postdoctoral workforce (Ghaffarzadegan et al., 2014), and new faculty hiring (Larson and Diaz, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Larson and Diaz, 2012).

claim: Educational disparities between students from URM and WR backgrounds begin early in life, and accumulate from K-12 through early independence.
source: Educational disparities between students from URM and WR backgrounds begin early in life, and accumulate from K-12 through early independence (National Institutes of Health, 2012b; Garrison, 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Institutes of Health, 2012b; Garrison, 2013).

claim: Differences in interest in faculty positions at research-intensive universities between URM and WR scientists remained when controlling for first-author publication rate, advisor relationships, PhD training institution, research self-efficacy, and training experiences.
source: Importantly, differences in interest in these assistant professor positions between URM and WR scientists remained when controlling for first-author publication rate, advisor relationships, PhD training institution, research self-efficacy, and training experiences (Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gibbs et al., 2014).

claim: Prominent scientists from URM backgrounds have written about the unique experiences, challenges, and biases (implicit and explicit) faced while conducting science in research-intensive environments.
source: Indeed, prominent scientists from URM backgrounds have written about the unique experiences, challenges, and biases (implicit and explicit) faced while conducting science in these environments (Colon Ramos and Quiñones-Hinojosa, 2016; Jarvis, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Colon Ramos and Quiñones-Hinojosa, 2016; Jarvis, 2015).

claim: There is an emerging body of literature on the distinct values that motivate many scientists from URM backgrounds to pursue scientific careers.
source: Further, there is an emerging body of literature on the distinct values that motivate many scientists from URM backgrounds to pursue scientific careers (e.g. giving back to or serving as a role model in their community of origin), the importance of congruence between personal values and career opportunities to fulfill them for scientists of all backgrounds, and the perception that faculty environments at research-intensive institutions such as medical schools may not enable sufficient engagement with the distinct values of URM scientists (Gibbs et al., 2013; Estrada et al., 2011; Thoman et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gibbs et al., 2013; Estrada et al., 2011; Thoman et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).

claim: On average, the pool of assistant professors turns over every six years.
source: On average, the pool of assistant professors turns over every six years.
evidence: Based on traditional academic promotion cycles as cited from Stanford University, 2016; Yale School of Medicine, 2014.

claim: In recent years, assistant professor hiring has been relatively stable at around 1000 positions each year.
source: The analysis presented here demonstrated that in recent years, assistant professor hiring has been relatively stable at around 1000 positions each year (or roughly 7 assistant professors per institution across all basic science departments annually).
evidence: Based on analysis of AAMC Faculty Roster data presented in the manuscript.

claim: To achieve parity with the pool of PhD graduates (estimated to grow to 10% URM in 2016) would require hiring around 100 URM assistant professors annually at medical schools.
source: Thus, to achieve parity with the pool of PhD graduates (estimated to grow to 10% URM in 2016) would require hiring around 100 URM assistant professors annually at medical schools.
evidence: Calculation based on the analysis of hiring trends and PhD graduate data.

claim: If roughly two-thirds of medical schools hired (and retained) just one faculty member from an URM background annually for the next six years, the system would reach parity with the PhD pool within one tenure cycle.
source: Put another way, if roughly two-thirds of medical schools hired (and retained) just one faculty member from an URM background annually for the next six years, the system would reach parity with the PhD pool within one tenure cycle.
evidence: Calculation based on the number of medical schools and hiring requirements to achieve parity.

claim: Available data suggest comparable postdoctoral transition rates across race/ethnicity for PhD graduates.
source: There are no reliable estimates on the number of postdocs in the US (currently or historically), thus these data were not included in the model (National Academy of Sciences NAoE, and Institute of Medicine, 2014). However, available data suggest comparable postdoctoral transition rates across race/ethnicity for PhD graduates (National Science Foundation, 2015b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Science Foundation, 2015b).

claim: 80% of Black and Hispanic science PhD graduates obtain their degrees from Carnegie classification research universities (high or very high research activity).
source: While 80% of Black and Hispanic science PhD graduates obtain their degrees from Carnegie classification research universities (high or very high research activity), this number is lower than the proportion of White and Asian PhD graduates from these institutions (90%) (National Science Foundation, 2015b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Science Foundation, 2015b).

claim: 90% of White and Asian PhD graduates obtain their degrees from Carnegie classification research universities (high or very high research activity).
source: While 80% of Black and Hispanic science PhD graduates obtain their degrees from Carnegie classification research universities (high or very high research activity), this number is lower than the proportion of White and Asian PhD graduates from these institutions (90%) (National Science Foundation, 2015b).
evidence: Cited from published literature (National Science Foundation, 2015b).

claim: Inequality and hierarchy characterize assistant professor hiring across disciplines.
source: However, a recent study has shown that inequality and hierarchy characterize assistant professor hiring across disciplines, and that prestige of doctoral institution plays a major role in who is hired (Clauset et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Clauset et al., 2015).

claim: Prestige of doctoral institution plays a major role in who is hired as assistant professors.
source: However, a recent study has shown that inequality and hierarchy characterize assistant professor hiring across disciplines, and that prestige of doctoral institution plays a major role in who is hired (Clauset et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Clauset et al., 2015).

claim: The model assumes all PhD graduates in the 'faculty aspire' stock pursue assistant professorships in research-intensive environments.
source: The model assumes all PhD graduates in the "faculty aspire" stock pursue assistant professorships in research-intensive environments.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that URM and WR candidates are hired in direct proportion to their representation on the market.
source: The model also posits that URM and WR candidates are hired in direct proportion to their representation on the market. That is, the model's output assumes that that racial bias does not impact hiring.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that differences in relative strength on the job market across URM status do not impact hiring.
source: Further, the model assumes that differences in relative strength on the job market across URM status do not impact hiring, because URM PhD graduates have lower interest in faculty careers in research-intensive environments than WR PhDs graduates even if they have graduated from the same institutions and have the same levels of scholarly productivity (Gibbs et al., 2015; Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure, justified by cited literature (Gibbs et al., 2015; Gibbs et al., 2014).

claim: The model assumes a fixed proportion of graduates would pursue and enter faculty positions in research-intensive environments ('faculty aspire').
source: Within each population, we assumed a fixed proportion of graduates would pursue and enter faculty positions in research-intensive environments (i.e. "faculty aspire").
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that efforts by the scientific community to enhance the diversity of the PhD pool would increase the pool of URM 'other aspire' PhDs.
source: We further assumed that efforts by the scientific community to enhance the diversity of the PhD pool ("URM target growth rate") would increase the pool of URM "other aspire" PhDs, some of whom will then transition to the faculty market.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that if the probability of being hired is relatively high (>20%) all candidates remain on the market that year; otherwise, one-fifth of the available pool drops out of the system.
source: Based on market hiring conditions, one-fifth of the candidates on the market drop out of the market annually. That is, if the probability of being hired is relatively high (>20%) all candidates remain on the market that year; otherwise, one-fifth of the available pool drops out of the system.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model structure.

claim: The average 'half-life' of a candidate on the market who is not hired is five years.
source: Thus, the average "half-life" of a candidate on the market who is not hired is five years (similar to the period of postdoctoral training for candidates pursuing faculty positions in research-intensive environments [National Institutes of Health, 2012a]).
evidence: This is derived from the model's dropout assumption and is consistent with cited literature (National Institutes of Health, 2012a).

claim: The model calibrated PhD graduations with R2=0.99, p<0.0001.
source: We calibrated our model against empirical trends in PhD graduations (R2=0.99, p<0.0001; Figure 4Ai) and chose the number of available slots to match empirical assistant professor hiring trends (R2=0.96, p<0.0001; Figure 4Aii).
evidence: Model validation results comparing model predictions to empirical data, as shown in Figure 4Ai.

claim: The model matched empirical assistant professor hiring trends with R2=0.96, p<0.0001.
source: We calibrated our model against empirical trends in PhD graduations (R2=0.99, p<0.0001; Figure 4Ai) and chose the number of available slots to match empirical assistant professor hiring trends (R2=0.96, p<0.0001; Figure 4Aii).
evidence: Model validation results comparing model predictions to empirical data, as shown in Figure 4Aii.

claim: The model is an 'abstract model' designed to examine the qualitative behavior associated with hypothetical policy outcomes.
source: Unlike a "facsimile model" that would be designed to explicitly predict precise values of outcome metrics (in this case, precise numbers of PhD graduate and assistant professor ratios), our model is an "abstract model," meaning that simulations are intended to examine the qualitative behavior associated with hypothetical policy outcomes, assuming that the system continues to follow its historic behavior (Gilbert, 2007).
evidence: This is a stated characterization of the model type, cited from Gilbert, 2007.

claim: From 1980-2013, the number of URM PhD graduates grew at an exponential rate.
source: Specifically, from 1980-2013, the number of URM PhD graduates grew at an exponential rate.
evidence: Based on analysis of National Science Foundation Survey of Earned Doctorates data.

claim: All model runs assumed continued exponential growth of URM PhD graduates.
source: Therefore, all model runs assumed continued exponential growth of URM PhD graduates (lower growth rates of PhD graduates did not change the qualitative behavior of our model's output).
evidence: This is a stated assumption for the model simulations.

claim: Lower growth rates of PhD graduates did not change the qualitative behavior of the model's output.
source: Therefore, all model runs assumed continued exponential growth of URM PhD graduates (lower growth rates of PhD graduates did not change the qualitative behavior of our model's output).
evidence: This is a stated result from sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: In all model runs, the percentage of PhD scientists from URM backgrounds is 13.8% in 2030 and 73% in 2080.
source: All model runs assume an exponential increase in the number of PhDs from URM backgrounds. Thus, in all runs, the percentage of PhD scientists from URM backgrounds is 13.8% in 2030 and 73% in 2080.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increasing the transition rate increased URM faculty representation by more than two-fold above what would be predicted from simply increasing the number of URM scientists exponentially through 2030.
source: That is, increasing the transition rate increased URM faculty representation by more than two-fold above what would be predicted from simply increasing the number of URM scientists exponentially through 2030.
evidence: Comparison of model simulation results with different transition rates, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of discrimination against URM scientists would attenuate any increases in faculty diversity.
source: These simulations assume no racial bias in hiring; the presence of discrimination against URM scientists would attenuate any increases in faculty diversity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how discrimination would affect the model's predictions.

claim: Broader changes in the biomedical academic labor market are insufficient to explain differences in faculty attainment between postdoctoral scientists from URM and WR backgrounds.
source: Therefore, broader changes in the biomedical academic labor market—i.e., more trainees than faculty positions, elongated pathways to independence, and declining research funding (Alberts et al., 2014; McDowell et al., 2014; Larson and Ghaffarzadegan, 2014)–are insufficient to explain differences in faculty attainment between postdoctoral scientists from URM and WR backgrounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis showing different hiring patterns for URM vs WR scientists despite both being subject to the same labor market conditions.

claim: Obtaining an assistant professorship position requires, at a minimum: (i) a position to be available; (ii) a candidate to be interested in and apply for the position; and (iii) the applicant to be favorably evaluated, offered the position and ultimately accept the position.
source: Obtaining an assistant professorship position requires, at a minimum: (i) a position to be available; (ii) a candidate to be interested in and apply for the position; and (iii) the applicant to be favorably evaluated, offered the position and ultimately accept the position.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the requirements for obtaining a faculty position.

claim: Systematic data on the applications, evaluations, offers and acceptances for assistant professor candidates in any academic discipline are not typically made available due to privacy and confidentiality laws.
source: Systematic data on the applications, evaluations, offers and acceptances for assistant professor candidates in any academic discipline are not typically made available (due to privacy and confidentiality laws), thus we were unable to include this information in the model.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability constraints.

claim: Part of the difference in faculty attainment can be attributed to the nature of the assistant professor hiring process itself, which emphasizes training background.
source: Thus, it is possible that part of the difference can be attributed to the nature of the assistant professor hiring process itself, which emphasizes training background.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited finding that prestige of doctoral institution plays a major role in hiring (Clauset et al., 2015) and the data showing different proportions of URM vs WR graduates from top-tier institutions.

claim: There are fundamental aspects of the environment, or nature of faculty work in research-intensive universities that cause otherwise equally qualified URMs to differentially choose other career paths.
source: This suggests that there are fundamental aspects of the environment, or nature of faculty work in research-intensive universities that cause otherwise equally qualified URMs to differentially choose other career paths.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited finding that interest differences persist even when controlling for qualifications (Gibbs et al., 2014).

claim: Faculty diversity efforts that rely primarily on enhancing rates of PhD graduates can only have their desired impact if they are coupled with efforts to get these candidates on the market and hired.
source: Thus, faculty diversity efforts that rely primarily on enhancing rates of PhD graduates (i.e. "filling the pipeline") can only have their desired impact if they are coupled with efforts to get these candidates on the market and hired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulation results showing that increasing the PhD pool alone does not increase faculty diversity.

claim: With concerted and targeted effort, higher diversity could be achieved relatively quickly among junior faculty.
source: While the challenge of achieving faculty diversity has been longstanding, with concerted and targeted effort, the numeric realities of assistant professor hiring and turnover mean that higher diversity could be achieved relatively quickly among junior faculty.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of hiring rates and turnover cycles.

claim: On average, assistant professor hiring has been relatively stable at roughly 7 assistant professors per institution across all basic science departments annually.
source: The analysis presented here demonstrated that in recent years, assistant professor hiring has been relatively stable at around 1000 positions each year (or roughly 7 assistant professors per institution across all basic science departments annually).
evidence: This is calculated from the total hiring numbers and the number of medical schools.

claim: Achieving parity with the PhD pool would still not reflect the proportion of people from URM backgrounds in the overall population (currently greater than 30%).
source: While this would still not reflect the proportion of people from URM backgrounds in the overall population (currently greater than 30%), this would represent a meaningful first step to addressing the longstanding goal of enhancing scientific excellence by increasing faculty diversity.
evidence: This is a comparison between projected faculty diversity and population demographics.

source: Biomedical PhD attainment data were obtained from the National Science Foundation's Survey of Earned Doctorates (SED), an annual census of individuals receiving research doctorates from accredited U.S. institutions (National Science Foundation, 2015a), as compiled by the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) (Garrison and Campbell, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the data source used in the study.

evidence: This is a description of the data source, cited from National Science Foundation, 2015a.

claim: The length of time that an individual occupied the position of assistant professor was assumed to be six years based on traditional academic promotion cycles.
source: To calculate the aggregate number of assistant professors hired each year, we made two assumptions: (i) the length of time that an individual occupied the position of assistant professor was six years based on traditional academic promotion cycles (Stanford University, 2016; Yale School of Medicine, 2014), and similarly, (ii) one-sixth of the WR and URM assistant professors left the rank of assistant professor in 1980 (either to become associate professors, or pursue other career options).
evidence: This is a stated assumption for the analysis, cited from Stanford University, 2016; Yale School of Medicine, 2014.

evidence: This is a stated assumption for the analysis, derived from the six-year tenure assumption.
